title: Hunter Goodman denies complaining about tilted Cardinals cap: ‘I never once mentioned the hat’
content:
In a twist to a saga that riled the baseball world, Colorado Rockies catcher Hunter Goodman on Saturday denied he said anything to umpire Doug Eddings about St. Louis Cardinals reliever Hancel Rincon’s cap, comments that came one day after the hat and its tilt were at the center of a confrontation between Cardinals manager Oli Marmol and Eddings.

“I never once mentioned the hat,” Goodman told reporters in Denver, according to MLB.com. “It doesn’t matter who’s pitching. I don’t care how they wear the hat. I’m trying to find out where the ball is coming out, and I’m trying to worry about what I’m doing in the box. I’m not worried about how his hat looks.”

The scene unfolded in the sixth inning on Friday night, when Rincon was making his MLB debut. He had a 2-0 count against Cole Carrigg with one out when Eddings instructed Cardinals catcher Leo Bernal, also a rookie, to tell Rincon to straighten his hat. Later in the inning, an irate Marmol approached Eddings and was tossed.

Goodman, who had come to the plate two batters earlier, was linked to the story in reports afterward, which indicated the catcher had pointed out the tilt of Rincon’s hat. But reports on Saturday were a bit murkier. MLB.com, for example, noted that Eddings did not use a batter’s name in his comments. The St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported: “Eddings’ explanation suggested this happened as Rincon began the inning and faced his first batter, the Rockies’ Hunter Goodman.”

“The batter said, ‘Hey, can he wear his hat like that?’” Eddings said Friday, according to the Post-Dispatch. “I really didn’t know, but it was really, really crooked. I asked the catcher to tell him to straighten his hat out, and the pitcher did.”

On Saturday, Goodman said he has taken heat because he was pulled into the dispute.

“I’ve been getting online stuff about me that I didn’t appreciate for something I didn’t say,” he said.

Marmol, whom Eddings ejected after he adjusted his cap while arguing with him on the field, told reporters that he thought Eddings’ actions were “embarrassing.”

“I thought it was poorly handled,” Marmol said Friday night, “and we’ll see what happens.”

The Major League Baseball Players Association was in touch with the players involved and with the commissioner’s office about the situation, another person close to the situation said Saturday. When asked for comment, an MLB spokesman pointed The Athletic to Eddings’ comments to reporters following Friday’s game. A message to the MLB Umpires Association went unanswered. No discipline for either Marmol or Eddings was announced.

The ejection and the outrage about Rincon’s hat simmered online afterward. In Denver, the Cardinals’ broadcast captured footage of St. Louis relievers, headed to the bullpen on Saturday night. Eddings, who was working third base, stopped Rincon and shook his hand. Some Cardinals players were also spotted with crooked caps ahead of the game.

The messy Friday night in Denver went viral on social media, with even Atlanta Braves Hall of Famer Chipper Jones and former All-Star center fielder Mike Cameron weighing in via posts on X.

“Ahhhh Doug Eddings…,” Jones wrote. “I believe I addressed his behavior and attitude a while back. Not surprising at all!”

“I’m sorry,” Cameron wrote, “there was no need for Doug Eddings’ commentary on a rookie and his cap… he was once a rookie and this isn’t his debut… if he wants to hold a standard it should be his own game.”

Minnesota Twins manager Derek Shelton said “yeah,” when asked if it was shocking to see Eddings’ directive to Rincon to adjust his hat.

“I will stop at that,” Shelton said.

“You know what? I wasn’t involved in that game,” New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. “I had a good conversation with the league about it when I saw it, though.”

It’s not an umpire’s job to play uniform police, Twins reliever Jeff Hoffman said.

“Who’s to say your hat’s not on tight enough?” Hoffman said. “Who’s to say your hat’s not straight enough? There’s more important things to spend your time on. To me, players are out there to play. Umpires are out there to umpire. That’s it.”

— Dan Hayes and Chris Kirschner contributed to this report.
